summary:
Mission Architect is a free, browser-based game, in which everyone may design, launch and run an entire space mission without needing to sign up or download anything. Users pick a scenario, then create their spaceship, instruments, orbit and launch vehicle, and ground communications. Real-time dashboard measures mass, power, budget, data, communications and time. After a review of the design, users launch their mission and get the simulation. Finally, they receive a report on whether their mission was successful or not.

The solution to this problem demonstrates how every decision leads to a consequence – adding a new instrument adds to power, data, mass and cost, and therefore, a bigger rocket is needed. Students form teams of up to four people and assume different roles to discuss these trade-offs.

It is important because designing a mission as a whole system is difficult to grasp for a beginner. This game allows students to see how real engineers solve these problems.
details:
Mission Architect is a web-based game, where the player designs and flies their space mission, using the same steps as NASA does. The player selects a mission scenario (CubeSat Earth observation, space telescope, lunar orbiter or Mars mission) and designs the spacecraft – bus, solar panels, batteries, antenna, attitude control and scientific payload. Then, the player selects the orbit and the launcher, and establishes the ground communications network. The dashboard shows the status of six resources – mass, power, budget, data, communications and time. The design review lists all the constraints the player violates – for instance, a battery too small to survive eclipse. Finally, the player launches and simulates the mission, which is impacted by some unpredictable events like solar flares or ground-station outage. The player receives the final score and a report of the success or failure reasons.

A rule engine ties all the subsystems together, so any change affects other subsystems. Adding an instrument means more power, data, mass and budget, leading to the need of a larger solar panel, heavier spacecraft and launcher. The game won't let the player to launch the mission if the spacecraft is too massive

Benefits

  • It is free, needs no install or login, and works on desktop and mobile.
  • Beginners can play with hints, while experienced players get tighter margins.
  • It explains why a decision works or fails, instead of only marking it right or wrong.
  • There is no single correct design, so players can try many solutions.

Intended impact

We want students and first-time learners to understand mission design as a connected system, so they see why real engineers constantly balance competing demands. It can be used in classrooms, clubs and outreach events, solo or in teams of up to four.

Tools and technology

  • Development: Google Antigravity
  • Frontend: [e.g. React, TypeScript, Vite]
  • 3D visualization: [e.g. three.js]
  • Team rooms: [e.g. Supabase or Firebase]
  • Hosting: [e.g. Netlify or Vercel]
  • Game data (instruments, orbits, launchers, scenarios) is stored as editable JSON, so new missions can be added without changing code.

NASA resources used

  • Design and Develop Science Missions: the launch, space, ground and user segments organize the game.
  • JPL Concept Maturity Levels: a progress bar from CML 1 to CML 4.
  • Mission Design Lab: the phases from concept to design review.
  • GMAT: the basis for orbit and trajectory values.
  • Mission Viz: inspiration for the 3D orbit view.
  • NASA’s telescope learning game and CubeSat 101: objective-driven instrument choices and the CubeSat scenario.

Creativity

  • The player’s design follows NASA’s own mission process rather than a generic game loop.
  • Team members take different roles (Mission Director, Spacecraft Engineer, Science Lead, Comms and Launch Lead) and must negotiate conflicts, and their coordination affects the score.
  • The post-mission report compares the player’s design to a real NASA mission.
  • [Add your signature feature here, e.g. a Ripple Graph or Mission Autopsy, if you built one.]

Factors we considered

  • Accessibility for players with no space background, through tooltips and plain-language explanations.
  • Realism versus simplicity: the physics is simplified, and we document what is simplified on a Data and Sources page.
  • Making judging easy: a quick-demo mode runs a full mission in about three minutes.
  • Fairness and replayability, with different difficulty levels and a seed option for reproducible runs.
  • Team balance, so each of the four roles has meaningful decisions
